## Overview

This course teaches a single discipline: how to turn a real technical system into
a short, educational **audio drama** — without ever abandoning the engineering
model underneath it.

You will begin by *experiencing* a finished audio story. Only after hearing the
result will you learn how it was constructed. This is the reverse-engineering
approach: experience first, deconstruct second, construct third.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Define technical storytelling and explain why audio drama is a useful medium for
  engineering education.
- Name the stages of the architectural principle pipeline and what each stage
  produces.
- Identify which stage of the pipeline is responsible for a given feature of a
  finished audio story.
- Recognize the foundational principle of this course.

## What is technical storytelling?

Technical storytelling is the disciplined practice of explaining a real technical
system through a narrative, without abandoning the engineering model underneath it.

It is not documentation read aloud. It is not a tutorial with characters added for
fun. It is a deliberate transformation of an engineering model into a form that a
listener can experience through the ear — dialogue, narration, sound effects, and
ambience.

## Why audio drama?

Audio is one of the most constrained media to write for. If the listener cannot
hear it, it does not exist. There is no screen to show a diagram, no cursor to
point at a component, no text to scroll past. Every important action must reach
the ear through at least one of: dialogue, narration, sound effect, ambience, or
music.

This constraint is a feature, not a limitation. It forces you to be precise about
what your system does and how it works. If you cannot explain it in sound, you
probably do not understand it well enough.

## The foundational principle

Every module in this course returns to one rule:

> *We do not simplify technology by abandoning its engineering model. We
> understand the model first, transform it deliberately, and use story to make
> that understanding accessible.*

Fiction is allowed. The facts underneath it are not.

## The architectural principle

The course follows a pipeline of distinct, inspectable stages:

```
Technical Model  ──▶  Metaphor  ──▶  Story  ──▶  Screenplay  ──▶  Audio Producer  ──▶  Audio Artifact
(WHAT IS TRUE)      (HOW EXPLAIN)  (HOW EXPERIENCE)  (HOW REPRESENT)  (HOW RENDER)       (RESULT)
```

Each stage has a clear job:

| Stage | Question it answers | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical Model | WHAT IS TRUE? | `concept.md` |
| Metaphor | HOW CAN WE EXPLAIN IT? | `metaphor.md` |
| Story | HOW CAN WE EXPERIENCE IT? | `scenes.md` |
| Screenplay | HOW DO WE REPRESENT IT? | `screenplay.md` |
| Audio Producer | HOW DO WE RENDER IT? | Audio artifact |

Each stage stays inspectable. This matters because errors can be traced back to
their origin: a technical error belongs in the model, a misleading analogy
belongs in the metaphor, confusing dialogue belongs in the story, and a bad
pronunciation belongs in rendering.

## The reverse-engineering approach

You will follow this learning loop:

```
EXPERIENCE    Hear the finished story
     ↓
DECONSTRUCT   Understand how it was built
     ↓
CONSTRUCT     Create your own
     ↓
REFLECT       Evaluate the transformation
```

First, you will hear the finished Crossplane restaurant audio story. Then you
will ask: *how did an architecture model become this?* Each subsequent module
reveals one more layer of the construction — from technical model, to metaphor,
to characters, to scenes, to screenplay.

## Listen to the reference example

Before reading any further, listen to the Crossplane restaurant audio story. You
will find the audio artifact linked from the [reference example](../../reference-example/concept.md).

Listen for:

- Which characters speak and what they say.
- Which sound effects you hear and when.
- What you learn about the technical system from the story.

You do not need to understand Crossplane to listen. The story is designed to be
followable without prior knowledge. You will reverse-engineer it in the modules
that follow.

## Benefits and risks

Storytelling can make technical content memorable and accessible. But it also
carries risks:

- **Metaphor drift** — the story becomes so entertaining that the listener
  forgets the technical model it represents.
- **Misconception injection** — the metaphor introduces ideas that contradict the
  real system.
- **Oversimplification** — the story drops important details to stay short or
  entertaining.

The course mitigates these risks through the architectural principle: every
transformation is documented and inspectable, and the technical model always
comes first.
